issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly describes the data as coming from a national probability/general population/nationally representative sample, but the Methods section states that participants were recruited from an introductory psychology participant pool and were predominantly 19-year-old students. This is a major contradiction that affects interpretation, external validity, and comparison to prior studies. Claims that the study improves on student-sample research by using a general population sample are therefore unsupported by the sample actually described.
issues.quote: Abstract: "We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment in a national probability sample over five years." ... Introduction: "We expand on Stanley et al.’s study by using a large, national probability sample spanning five years" ... Method: "We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington." ... "Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1"

issues.description: The manuscript claims national representativeness and high generalizability to New Zealand, but the described sample is a young, predominantly female, predominantly Pākehā student sample from one university participant pool. This severely limits external validity and invalidates claims about the general population or national attitudes.
issues.quote: "Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population."

issues.description: The stated focal construct shifts between environmental concern and willingness to sacrifice/behavioral change. The abstract and introduction emphasize willingness to change behavior, the measures section defines environmentalism as concern about environmental problems, and one listed item reflects skepticism/exaggeration rather than sacrifice behavior. These are not interchangeable constructs; concern, denial, and willingness to sacrifice capture different psychological domains. This mismatch undermines construct validity and interpretation of findings.
issues.quote: Abstract: "people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment" ... Current Study: "people’s willingness to change their behaviour to protect the environment" ... Measures: "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'" ... Data Analysis: "We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment."

issues.description: The manuscript labels the environmental variable as 'willingness to sacrifice,' 'willingness to make sacrifices,' 'environmentalism,' and 'concern about environmental problems' despite giving only two concern/skepticism items in Methods. This internal inconsistency makes it unclear what variable was actually analyzed and whether Table 1/Figure 1 correspond to the described measure.
issues.quote: "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems." ... Table 1 note: "WILL = willingness to make sacrifices for the environment." ... Results: "SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice"

issues.subcategory: inadequate sample size for complex longitudinal CLPM
issues.description: The analysis estimates a highly complex five-wave path model with three constructs and item-level residual constraints, yet the analytic sample is only 374 participants. Given likely attrition across five years and a model with 2279 degrees of freedom, this sample is likely underpowered and unstable for precise estimation of small cross-lagged effects, especially with listwise deletion.
issues.quote: "Of the 374 participants included in this study" ... "Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73"

issues.description: The authors use listwise deletion for a five-wave longitudinal study, which can substantially reduce effective sample size and bias estimates unless data are missing completely at random. No justification, missingness diagnostics, attrition analyses, or sensitivity analyses are provided. Full-information maximum likelihood would generally be preferable.
issues.quote: "Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion."

issues.description: The manuscript explicitly says full retention details are available elsewhere rather than reporting them in the paper. For a five-wave longitudinal study, readers need wave-specific Ns, retention percentages, reasons for dropout if known, and comparisons of retained vs. lost participants to assess bias. Omitting these prevents evaluation of attrition threats.
issues.quote: "Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website."

issues.description: One RWA item was not assessed at time two, creating planned missingness/non-equivalent measurement across waves. The manuscript does not explain how this was handled psychometrically or analytically, whether the latent construct was adjusted, or whether comparability across time was evaluated.
issues.quote: "The item 'Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done', was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points."

issues.description: Environmentalism appears to be measured with only two items, one indexing concern and one indexing perceived exaggeration. A two-item measure provides limited content coverage and may conflate concern with skepticism/denial. It does not adequately operationalize the broad construct 'environmentalism' or 'willingness to sacrifice.'
issues.quote: "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'"

issues.description: The manuscript does not report whether reverse-coded items were reversed, how composite scores were computed, whether item parcels or latent variables were used, or how the environmentalism variable was constructed from the listed items. This omission prevents replication and interpretation.
issues.quote: "Three items favoured dominance ... and three favoured equality" ... "These included items such as ..." ... "Environmentalism was measured ..."

issues.description: Reliability is discussed vaguely, but coefficients are only indirectly visible in Table 1 and only for Time 1. Longitudinal analyses require reliability or measurement quality at each wave. The manuscript does not report alpha/omega across all five time points or for the environmental measure.
issues.quote: "Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used"

issues.description: The authors impose stationarity/equality constraints over time but do not test longitudinal measurement invariance of SDO, RWA, or environmentalism. Without establishing at least metric/scalar invariance, interpreting autoregressive and cross-lagged paths as comparable over time is problematic because changes may reflect shifting measurement properties rather than true score dynamics.
issues.quote: "We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant."

issues.description: The model constrains cross-lagged effects to be identical across all intervals because the authors were more interested in overall effects. This strong assumption may be false over a five-year period and can mask temporal heterogeneity. The manuscript provides no empirical test or comparison to less constrained models to justify stationarity.
issues.quote: "We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured."

issues.description: The description of model constraints is confusing and possibly incorrect. It says residual variance for the same item over time was constrained equal, but the analysis is introduced as path analysis on three variables across five points, not an item-level SEM. It is unclear whether item-level latent factors or scale scores were modeled. This ambiguity prevents evaluating whether the model was appropriate.
issues.quote: "The model included three variables across five measurement points" ... "We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points."

issues.subcategory: incorrect parameter notation using SD instead of SE
issues.description: Regression/path estimates are reported with 'SD' accompanying coefficients, apparently where standard errors should be reported. Standard deviations are not the relevant uncertainty metric for regression coefficients. This is a statistical reporting error that obscures inferential precision.
issues.quote: "SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001" ... "RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001"

issues.description: Several chi-square difference/Wald-type results omit the chi-square symbol or are malformed (e.g., '2(1)' instead of 'χ2(1)'). This creates ambiguity about what test was actually used and suggests reporting errors in the inferential statistics.
issues.quote: "We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126" ... "the lagged effect on SDO was stronger than the reverse (2(1) = 39.97, p < .001)" ... "These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)"

issues.subcategory: incorrect interpretation of nonsignificant model comparison
issues.description: The authors compare a model constraining SDO and RWA paths equal to an unconstrained model and obtain a nonsignificant difference test (p = .126), which means they failed to detect a difference. Yet they still conclude SDO is a stronger predictor based on coefficient magnitude alone. This is an inferential error.
issues.quote: "We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor"

issues.subcategory: claim of significant difference contradicts nonsignificant test
issues.description: The Discussion states that SDO is a 'significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA,' but the Results report a nonsignificant equality-constraint comparison (p = .126). This directly contradicts the reported inferential test.
issues.quote: Results: "2(1) = 2.34, p = .126" ... Discussion: "SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA."

issues.subcategory: causal claims from observational cross-lagged data
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly treats cross-lagged associations from observational survey data as evidence of causation. Cross-lagged panel models with no experimental manipulation and limited control for confounders do not establish causality, especially when stable trait confounding and omitted variables are plausible. This overstates what the design can support.
issues.quote: Abstract: "These findings suggest that the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance" ... Discussion: "These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism." ... "this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes"

issues.subcategory: third-variable confounding acknowledged but not addressed
issues.description: The Discussion itself notes that a third variable could explain the bidirectional associations, but the analysis does not include any covariates or alternative models. This unaddressed confounding undermines the causal interpretation and should have been incorporated into design/analysis rather than only post hoc acknowledged.
issues.quote: "a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable."

issues.subcategory: no control variables in longitudinal model
issues.description: No demographic, political, socioeconomic, or contextual covariates are included, despite many plausible confounds for ideology and environmentalism. In observational panel data, failing to account for such variables leaves cross-lagged paths vulnerable to omitted-variable bias.
issues.quote: "We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment."

issues.description: The manuscript provides no preregistration, analysis plan, or clear statement of whether modeling decisions were confirmatory or exploratory. Given multiple modeling choices (stationarity constraints, equality constraints, deletion method, handling of missing item at time 2), undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom are a concern.
issues.quote: "A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript."

issues.description: The syntax will only be made available upon acceptance, meaning reviewers and readers cannot inspect the exact model specification during evaluation. Reproducibility is further limited by not reporting sufficient details in the manuscript itself.
issues.quote: "A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript."

issues.description: The claim that a traditional Wald test is not possible because of model constraints is questionable. Equality of parameters in SEM is routinely testable via Wald or likelihood-ratio/difference testing even in constrained models. The statement suggests either misunderstanding or poor explanation of the statistical procedure.
issues.quote: "Due to the nature of the analysis and the constraints placed on the model, the traditional Wald test to confirm that SDO is a statistically stronger predictor than RWA is not possible."

issues.description: The reported chi-square difference of 15,389.13 with 1 df for comparing lagged effects is implausibly enormous relative to the tiny coefficients described, suggesting a transcription, scaling, or reporting error. Such an extreme statistic warrants verification and undermines confidence in the reported results.
issues.quote: "These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)"

issues.description: The RMSEA point estimate and confidence interval are inconsistent: a point estimate of .03 should not have a 90% CI of [.025, .026], whose upper bound is below .03. This appears to be a reporting error.

The model is accepted despite poor CFI (.86), based on RMSEA/SRMR and a claim that some indices are 'less influenced by complexity.' This selective emphasis is questionable, especially with complex SEM and possible misspecification. The manuscript should justify fit criteria a priori and discuss poor comparative fit rather than simply accepting the model.
issues.quote: "Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03 ... SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted."

issues.description: The manuscript references Figure 1 for unstandardized parameters but does not provide the figure content in the text supplied, and does not report all autoregressive and cross-lagged coefficients, standard errors, or confidence intervals. Full results are necessary to evaluate model adequacy and replication.
issues.quote: "Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL)."

issues.description: The authors state that the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than RWA's based on non-overlapping confidence intervals. However, non-overlap of separate CIs is not the proper test for comparing dependent correlations that share a variable. This is both an inferential problem and an inconsistency in interpretation.
issues.quote: "the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than the correlation for RWA, as indicated by the non-overlapping confidence interval."

issues.subcategory: improper comparison of dependent correlations via CI overlap
issues.description: Using non-overlapping confidence intervals to conclude one correlation is stronger than another is not a valid test, particularly for dependent correlations sharing a common variable. A formal test (e.g., Steiger's test) would be needed.
issues.quote: "the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than the correlation for RWA, as indicated by the non-overlapping confidence interval."

issues.description: Table 1 reports 95% confidence intervals 'based on 1000 iterations,' but does not state what was iterated (bootstrap?), how resampling was done, or why this method was used for descriptive statistics/correlations. This is insufficiently transparent.
issues.quote: "Numbers in square brackets represent 95% confidence intervals based on 1000 iterations."

issues.description: Both SDO and RWA are measured using only six items each from much longer scales, and the authors admit reliability is poorer than typical. Shortened measures may not adequately capture the breadth of the constructs and can attenuate or distort cross-lagged estimates.
issues.quote: "Social dominance orientation was assessed using six items from Sidanius and Pratto’s [1] SDO6 scale." ... "Right-wing authoritarianism was assessed with six items from Altemeyer’s [27] RWA scale." ... "Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used"

issues.subcategory: domain mismatch between theory and measure
issues.description: The theoretical discussion concerns environmentalism, climate change denial, policy support, exploitation, and behavior, but the operational measure appears to be a narrow two-item concern/exaggeration scale. The broad theoretical conclusions about exploitation and mitigation are not well matched to this narrow outcome measure.
issues.quote: "These findings suggest that the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance" ... "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems"

issues.description: The manuscript infers specific motivations (desire to dominate nature; submit to authority) from associations between ideology scales and a limited environmental attitude measure. These motivational claims are not directly measured and go beyond what the data can support.
issues.quote: "These findings suggest that the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to tradition and authority."

issues.subcategory: cross-lagged panel model interpreted as directionality disentanglement
issues.description: The paper states that the analyses 'help us disentangle the directionality of the relationships.' Traditional CLPMs confound between-person stability with within-person change and are not sufficient to identify directional within-person processes. More appropriate approaches (e.g., RI-CLPM) are not considered.
issues.quote: "These analyses help us disentangle the directionality of the relationships"

issues.subcategory: failure to model random intercepts/stable trait confounding
issues.description: The use of a standard cross-lagged panel model without random intercepts means stable between-person differences can generate apparent cross-lagged effects. Given ideology and environmental attitudes are highly stable, this is a serious modeling limitation that can bias interpretation of temporal influence.
issues.quote: "We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant."

issues.subcategory: sample source inconsistent with cited data infrastructure
issues.description: The manuscript mentions both a Victoria University introductory psychology pool and the NZAVS website/team, implying use of NZAVS data. These are very different sampling frames. The paper never clearly explains whether the study used a local student panel, NZAVS, or both, producing major confusion about provenance of the data.
issues.quote: "We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington." ... "Full details about the sample... are available on the NZAVS website." ... "We express our gratitude to the New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study (NZAVS) team"

issues.description: The paper refers to five semesters from 2009 to 2013 and also to a five-year analysis/five time points, but does not clearly specify exact measurement dates or intervals between waves. Stationary lag assumptions require knowledge of equal spacing; 'five semesters' also suggests nonannual spacing inconsistent with 'five-year'.
issues.quote: "participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013)."

issues.subcategory: five semesters vs five years inconsistency
issues.description: The manuscript title and framing present a five-year panel, but the Methods section says five semesters from 2009 to 2013. Five semesters is not the same as five annual waves and implies unequal or shorter intervals. This inconsistency matters for interpreting lagged effects and stationarity.
issues.quote: "A five-year cross-lagged analysis" ... "across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013)."

issues.subcategory: unclear whether observed or latent variables were analyzed
issues.description: The paper alternates between item-level discussion and variable-level path analysis but never specifies whether SDO/RWA/environmentalism were modeled as latent factors or observed composites. This distinction is crucial for interpreting fit indices, residual constraints, and treatment of measurement error.
issues.quote: "The model included three variables across five measurement points" ... "we also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time"

issues.subcategory: sample demographic narrowness unacknowledged in conclusions
issues.description: The sample is heavily skewed toward young adults, women, and Pākehā participants, yet the conclusions are framed broadly about 'those in the general population' and 'New Zealanders.' These demographic imbalances limit generalizability and should be acknowledged directly.
issues.quote: "the average age was 19 years at Time 1 ... 68% were female ... the majority (86%) identified as Pākehā" ... "The take home message from our study is that for those in the general population"

issues.subcategory: unsupported sociopolitical interpretation of national ideology
issues.description: The manuscript infers from the cross-lag pattern that 'New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.' This is a sweeping sociocultural claim not directly tested and especially untenable given the actual sample appears to be university students rather than New Zealanders broadly.
issues.quote: "Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance."
